We can produce now.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>## Quick‑Guide to Japanese Business Etiquette *(Every point below is a “rule of thumb” that will help you avoid faux‑pas and build respect.)* | # | What to Do | Why It Matters | Practical Tips | |---|------------|---------------|----------------| | **1. Arrive on time (or a bit early)** | Punctuality is a core Japanese value. Being late signals lack of respect and can be seen as rash. | Arrive 5–10 min early. If you can’t, call and apologize in Japanese. | | **2. Use modest, formal greetings** | Bowing is the traditional non‑verbal greeting that shows respect and acknowledges hierarchy. | 1‑2 cm bow for a casual greeting; 30° for formal. 1–2 cm is acceptable for handshake & bow. | | **3. Master the business‑card (meishi) etiquette** | Meishi is as important as a résumé. Treat it like a sacred document. | • Keep the card in a clean holder.
• Receive it with two hands, read it, then put it back carefully in a holder.
• Do not write on the card until the end of the meeting. | | **4. Respect the hierarchy** | Japanese teams are strongly hierarchical; decisions often come from the top. | Address the senior as *‑san* (e.g., Tanaka‑san) and use the correct title.
Ask to speak with the senior person first. | | **5. Keep conversation polite and indirect** | Directness (“no”) can be perceived as rude or confrontational. | Use softening phrases: “If it’s suitable,…”? and “I was thinking…” rather than “I refuse.” | | **6. Observe meeting etiquette** | The order, seating, and conduct signifies respect and harmony. | • Be seated by the person who invites you.
• Don’t interrupt; let everyone finish speaking before you speak.
• Take notes quietly. | | **7. Dress conservatively** | Business attire is typically dark, conservative, and immaculate. | • Dark business suit, plain tie, no bright socks.
• Avoid overly flashy accessories. | | **8. Gift‑giving (“oiwake”)** | A small gift shows respect but should not be lavish or show the price. | • Bring a small, tasteful hamper or something presumably useful.
• Wrap it in a plain, clean Japanese‐style wrapping; no red paper (that’s for chan‑sen “rebirth”).
• Do not reveal the cost; the value should be implicit. | | **9. Email & written communication** | Emails are polite and concise. | • Use proper salutations: “Dear Mr./Ms. Tanaka” followed by “Yoroshiku onegaishimasu” (please treat me well).
• Keep the subject line respectful.
• Avoid emoticons and overly casual language. | | **10. Avoid public displays of emotion** | Emotion can be seen as a lack of control, especially in business. | • Maintain a calm, even tone.
• Do not shout or gesticulate excessively. | | **11. Never accept a “cheer” (飲み会) on the spot** | It’s fine after you’ve established a relationship and trust. | • Observe the group’s dynamic first.
• Leave a polite thank‑you note for the invitation. | | **12. Follow up with a prompt thank‑you** | A thank‑you note reinforces respect and moves the relationship forward. | • Send a handwritten card if possible; otherwise a short email.
• Explicitly state the meeting’s key points for clarity. | | **13. Don’t start conversations about politics or religion** | These are taboo topics in business. | • Stick to neutral topics like politics, business, local culture. | | **14. Use the “Nemawashi” (background groundwork) approach** | Getting informal consensus before formal meetings is common. | • Arrange intro calls or informal dinners to gain support before hitting the board. | | **15. Mind your physical space** | Personal space is respected. | • Avoid standing too close during a meeting to avoid invasion of personal space. | | **16. Leave all cell phone notifications off** | Phone rings, especially when the phone is a side‑table, can be a rude interruption. | • Keep your phone on silent; let the host handle any calls. | | **17. Return business cards pound‑wise** | Passing by a stack of cards can be seen as careless. | • Use a small card holder or a neat pile in a conspicuous place. | | **18. Consent for leaving the office** | Concluding a meeting shows etiquette - thanking or kindly closing. | • “Thank you for your time, I will follow up next week.” | ### Quick “Do’s & Don’ts” - **Do** – Practice a respectful bow, keep business cards simple, show respect for age and titles. - **Don’t** – Show up late, use a casual name, write on a digital card, use the first name, or mention money or price. --- #### A Few “Inside” Tips for Real‑World Success | Scenario | What You’ll Do | Why It Works | |----------|----------------|--------------| | **First Meeting** | Bring a small box of high‑quality items (e.g., Japanese decorative pens or citrus). | It signals respect and shows you value this relationship. | | **During a Meeting** | Keep your left hand on the table, rights free for notes. | Avoids distraction and is seen as professional. | | **Negotiating** | Let decisions surface “outside both of us” rather than with “I am the boss.” | Shows humility and a team‑oriented mindset. | | **Leaving the Office** | Offer a soft “Arigatou gozaimashita” (thank you for how the room ended). | A polite closing note in the conversation smooths the exit. | --- ### Bottom Line Japan’s business culture offers a calm, methodical, and respectful rhythm. By mastering etiquette—**preparing on time, honoring hierarchy, handling business cards like a craft, and keeping communication tight and respectful—you’ll instantly boost your professional credibility and establish a rapport that often lasts beyond one meeting.**
